analysis.one_liner: Lets people erase their personal data from all data brokers with one request to the FTC.
analysis.headline: The DELETE Act, with bipartisan sponsorship from three House members, never received a committee vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a government-run website where anyone could make one request to have their personal information deleted from every registered data broker — companies that buy and sell details about people they have no direct relationship with. Data brokers would have to register with the Federal Trade Commission, check a secure hashed registry at least every 31 days, delete matching records within 31 days, pay fees to fund the system, and pass independent audits every three years. The FTC would enforce violations like unfair or deceptive practices, and state privacy laws giving stronger protection would remain in force.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose names, addresses, phone numbers, browsing histories, locations, and inferred traits are compiled and sold by data brokers without their knowledge. The bill gives them a single free request to delete that data everywhere, instead of hunting down dozens of opt-out forms. It also benefits victims of stalking, identity theft, and people whose sensitive information (health status, religion, pregnancy) gets traded commercially.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose data is brokered and sold

how_it_helps.text: Creates a centralized FTC system where a single request deletes a person's information from all registered data brokers and stops future collection [S2].
Requires every data broker to register annually with the FTC and disclose what it collects, its sources, and its opt-out method, with the registry posted in a machine-readable public format [S2].

Requires brokers to check secure hashed registries at least every 31 days and delete matching records within 31 days, submitting deletion counts to the FTC, and to undergo independent third-party audits every three years [S2].
Protects stronger state privacy laws from being overridden, and funds the system through capped broker fees rather than new taxes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the broader data-for-advertising ecosystem, which would lose the ability to sell personal profiles of people who opt out. The bill also creates real costs for the FTC, but the bill caps broker subscription fees to cover the system's operating cost, so the industry funds the machinery that polices it.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts trade secrets from the disclosure requirements, which data brokers could invoke to keep much of their sourcing and sales information confidential [S2].

The definition excludes consumer reporting agencies, fraud-prevention uses, and publicly available professional information, so some firms handling equally sensitive data would operate outside the deletion right [S2].

The centralized system requires the FTC to hold hashed copies of people's emails, phone numbers, and addresses, which security experts generally note concentrates sensitive identifiers in one database that would become a high-value target [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most people the benefit is clear: a real, enforceable right to erase data held by companies they never chose to deal with, at no cost to taxpayers since broker fees fund the system. The design has genuine weak points — trade-secret carve-outs, industry exclusions, and the security risk of the FTC's own hashed registries — but these are refinement problems, not reasons the bill fails on its merits. The honest cost is borne by a profitable industry that would lose inventory.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and a subcommittee in June 2023, never got a markup or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Lori Trahan introduced the bill on June 22, 2023, with Rep. Chuck Edwards as an original cosponsor, making the introduction bipartisan [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce [S4].
The bill never advanced beyond that referral: no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action is recorded in its full action history [S4].
The bill drew three cosponsors in total — two House Democrats and one House Republican — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers come out ahead: with the bill never reaching a vote, they kept selling personal profiles with no federal one-stop deletion right and no mandatory registration or audits. Ordinary people gained nothing because the bill never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers who kept selling profiles

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor with two Democratic and one Republican cosponsors — but the Republican-controlled committee that held the bill took no recorded action, so no vote ever revealed where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill strikes at the core of the data-brokerage business: a single consumer request would force deletion of profiles these companies build on people who never had a relationship with them, and the annual registration, public disclosure, audits, and fees would expose an industry that currently operates largely in the shadows. Blocking the bill preserves that revenue.

Targeted advertising depends on brokered profiles of individuals; mass deletion requests and an end to future collection would shrink the audience data available for purchase. The industry's gain from the bill's defeat is ordinary people's continued loss of control over their own information.
